views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the negotiating table and keep the de-escalation track alive — continue the purchase and currency commitments already on the table and work toward a Mar-a-Lago summit deal, but hold firm on the structural IP/tech-transfer and subsidy demands that would hollow out our industrial policy and tech self-sufficiency. Do not escalate further, as retaliation would deepen the damage to our already-battered export sector and risk a move back to a 25% tariff; equally, do not fully concede structural reform, which touches core sovereignty and Made in China 2025 objectives.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is high but not existential (threat_score +0.4). Exports plunged 20.7% in February — the worst month in three years — and exports to the US fell 14.1% in Jan-Feb under the ~$250B of US tariffs, with ANZ describing 'China's trade recession has started to emerge'; this is a major export-sector hit in the +0.5 anchor range. Firm-level targeting is real: the US unsealed charges against Huawei and formally requested Meng Wanzhou's extradition (Jan 28), and condemned 'deliberate political suppression.' US demands on forced technology transfer, IP, and subsidies also threaten the tech-autonomy and CCP-legitimacy elements in the +1.0 anchor. But the situation has de-escalated since December: Trump suspended the 10%->25% hike twice (Dec 1 G20, Feb 24) citing 'substantial progress,' Lighthizer called a deal 'very close,' and a Xi-Trump signing summit is planned — so this is not existential and the US is negotiating under its own time pressure (contrasted with China's stated willingness to buy billions in soybeans, beef, and LNG and a currency non-devaluation pledge). That justifies the mild positive action stance (action_score +0.15, 'negotiate'): continue engaging and trading purchase concessions, but guard the structural red lines, since ceding forced-tech-transfer and subsidy reform outright would be the one outcome that genuinely damages our long-term technological and political position.
key_factors: February exports -20.7% YoY, worst in three years, US-bound exports -14.1%
~$250B of US Section 301 tariffs in force; List 3 hike to 25% suspended twice
Huawei/Meng firm-level targeting: US charges + extradition request (Jan 28)
US structural demands (forced tech transfer, IP, subsidies) threaten industrial policy
De-escalatory track: talks progressing, tariff hike delayed, Xi-Trump summit planned
China already committed to large purchase increases and currency non-devaluation

US DOJ unseals fraud/sanctions charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests extradition.

Exports to the US fell 14.1% to $52.3B in first two months; US trade surplus $42B; ANZ: trade recession emerging.
Trump delays tariff hike citing progress; enforcement mechanism remains major sticking point; Xi-Trump summit to conclude.
Trump delays tariff deadline; China agreed to billions in purchases but resisted structural changes.
